Both editions can hand an alert to an AI agent that you run, and Lite lets the agent read and report. Darling can also let it change alert settings (mutes, custom alert rules and thresholds). On a server, it can force or unforce a Query Store plan or evict a cached plan. It can recompile a module, create or drop a plan guide, or kill a session. Each of these has its own switch per server, and all are off until you turn them on. Darling records every change. A person can undo alert-setting changes, plan forces and plan guide changes. A plan eviction, a recompile or a session kill cannot be undone. Agent dispatch explains the levels.
The Dashboard edition is deprecated. Existing installs keep working, but we recommend Lite or Darling for new deployments. Choosing an edition compares all three.

Each release ships these downloads. For Lite, a `Setup.exe` and a portable ZIP. For Darling, the service ZIP (with the viewer inside), a Viewer `Setup.exe` for a remote seat, and the Linux and Compose tarballs. The Full Dashboard and its CLI installer ship nothing. Their last builds are in the v3.2.0 release.
1. Download `PerformanceMonitorLite-lite-Setup.exe`. It is a self-contained build, so you do not install a .NET runtime first.
Data starts to flow within 1 to 5 minutes. The monitoring login needs `VIEW SERVER STATE` (Permissions).

Before you upgrade an older install with `Setup.exe`, read the warning in the Lite guide. On versions older than 3.4.0, `Setup.exe` deletes the data in the install directory (see Upgrading an install older than 3.4.0). The Lite guide also covers the portable ZIP, collectors, storage, and configuration.

1. Download `PerformanceMonitorDarling-<version>.zip` and `SHA256SUMS.txt` from the latest release. Check the zip hash against `SHA256SUMS.txt`. The zip carries its own .NET runtime, so there is nothing to install first.

2. Extract the zip to `C:\Program Files\PerformanceMonitorDarling`. Do not use your Desktop, Downloads, or any folder under `C:\Users\`. The service runs as a virtual account that cannot read a user profile (why).
5. Add your first server in the viewer. `darling.json` is only a seed. The service reads it on its first start, so a server added to the file later is ignored (why).

Install Darling gives each step with the log line or screen that proves it worked. To upgrade, run `upgrade-darling.ps1`. To remove the service, run `uninstall-darling.ps1`. Both are in the install folder. For Linux and the web dashboard, read the Darling quick start. The Darling operator guide is the configuration reference.

|**PostgreSQL syntax + PGWire**|Use familiar SQL, `psql`, DBeaver, and PostgreSQL drivers, including prepared queries and transactions.|
|**Live queries**|Subscribe to SQL results over WebSocket and keep your UI current as matching rows change.|

|**Server functions**|Run JavaScript and compiled TypeScript inside the embedded V8 runtime. Invoke backend logic through SQL, HTTP, or generated clients and inside a DB Trasaction with commit and rollback|
|**Durable pub/sub**|Turn table changes into events for workers, integrations, and agents, with consumer groups, acknowledgements, and retries.|
|**Auth + access control**|Use authentication and row-level policies for shared data. Manage your backend through the included admin UI.|
|**Tables partitioned by user**|Create `USER` tables so each person's rows live in their own partition. Use `SHARED` tables for data everyone reads, and `STREAM` tables for events that expire.|
|**Tiered storage**|Keep recent rows in RocksDB. Flush older user and shared data to compressed Parquet on disk or object storage, and query both tiers as one table.|
|**Typed app APIs**|Generate TypeScript and Dart/Flutter table and function contracts from your SQL schema.|
|**Raft clustering**|Run multiple nodes with replicated data, leader election, and live subscriptions served by each node.|
Run the server with a native binary or Docker.
For a smaller starting point, run `kalam init` in an empty folder and choose a minimal template. See the quick-start guide for setup details and demo credentials.

KalamDB implements PostgreSQL compatibility on its own Rust engine, powered by DataFusion and Arrow. Migration suitability depends on the SQL features and extensions your application uses; see the SQL reference and release notes.

The SDK delivers the initial rows and maintains the current result as inserts, updates, and deletes arrive. Writes through PGWire, HTTP, or server functions feed the same live-query system. See the TypeScript SDK and React bindings.
